questions.q: In C, every function argument is passed by value: the parameter gets a copy of its argument's value.
questions.explain: C passes all arguments by value. Even with pass by pointer, the parameter gets a copy of the argument's value. That value just happens to be an address.
Parameter a gets a copy of b's value. Assigning 5 to a changes only the copy, so b is still 1.

questions.q: If a function assigns its pointer parameter to point to a different address, the caller's argument now points to that new address as well.
questions.explain: The pointer parameter is a copy of the argument's address value. Changing where the parameter points does not change the argument's value.
p starts with x's address, but `p = &z;` points the copy at z instead. `*p = 9` then writes into z, not x, so x stays 3.

questions.q: In the pass-by-pointer pattern, what value does the pointer parameter get?
choices: A copy of the value stored in the caller's variable
The address of a storage location passed in by the caller
A new variable that is copied back to the caller when the function returns
The name of the caller's variable
questions.explain: The parameter gets the value of an address, for example the address of one of the caller's local variables. Dereferencing it reaches that storage location.

questions.q: Given `int change_value(int *input);` and `int x;`, which call lets change_value modify x?
choices: `change_value(x);`
`change_value(&x);`
`change_value(*x);`
`change_value(int *x);`
questions.explain: The parameter type is `int *`, so the argument must be the address of an int variable. `&x` is the address of x.

questions.q: Inside `int change_value(int *input)`, which statement stores 100 in the caller's variable that input points to?
choices: `input = 100;`
`int *input = 100;`
questions.explain: Dereferencing with `*input` refers to the location input points to, so `*input = 100;` assigns 100 there. `input = 100;` would change the pointer itself.

questions.q: If a function's parameter is declared `int *input`, what must the caller pass as the argument?
choices: Any int value
The address of an int variable
The address of any variable, whatever its type
A pointer to a pointer to an int
questions.explain: An `int *` parameter points to an int, so the address passed must be the address of an int variable.

questions.q: Which statements about passing a pointer parameter are true?
choices: Dereferencing the parameter lets the function change memory the caller can see after the function returns
The parameter gets a copy of the argument's value, which is an address
Assigning a new address to the parameter changes the caller's argument
The parameter and its argument refer to the same memory location
questions.explain: The parameter holds a copy of the argument's address, so both refer to the same memory, and writing through `*param` changes it. Reassigning the parameter changes only the copy.

questions.q: Which operator do you put in front of a variable name to pass that variable's address to a function?
questions.explain: `&x` evaluates to the address of x, as in `change_value(&x);`.
val gets 30, which is less than 100, so `*input = 100` writes 100 into x through the pointer.
The function returns val, which is the original value of x (30). So the program prints `x: 100 y: 30`.
val gets 150, which is not less than 100, so `*input = val * 2` stores 300 in x.
change_value always returns the original value it read through the pointer, here 150.

questions.q: In the change_value example, what does the statement `val = *input;` do?
choices: Stores the address in input into val
Gives val the value stored at the location input points to
Makes input point to val
Copies val into the caller's variable
questions.explain: `*input` dereferences the pointer, so val gets the int stored at that address (x's value in main).

questions.q: Just before change_value returns (called as `change_value(&x)` from main), where is the memory that its parameter input points to?
choices: In change_value's own stack frame
In main's stack frame, where local variable x lives
In a temporary copy that is discarded when change_value returns
Nowhere; input stores an int value, not an address
questions.explain: input holds the address of x, a local variable in main's stack frame. That is why writing through input changes x after the function returns.

questions.q: When an array is passed to a function, what does the array parameter get?
choices: A copy of every element in the array
The base address of the passed array
Only the value of the first element
The number of elements in the array
questions.explain: An array parameter gets the value of the array's base address, so it refers to the same elements as its argument.

questions.q: A function can change the values stored in an array argument, and the caller sees those changes after the function returns.
questions.explain: The parameter refers to the same array elements as the argument (it holds the base address), so changes to the elements are visible to the caller. Pass by pointer works the same way.
